documents.abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.

This study explores the pedagogical aspects of artificial intelligence (AI) application in tourism education. It presents a comparative analysis of empirical studies focusing on the integration of AI technologies into the educational process in higher education institutions. The research examines the opportunities and challenges of using AI in tourism education, with particular attention to teaching methods, personalized learning, student engagement, digital competencies, and the development of professional skills. The study aims to identify current trends in AI-supported education and evaluate its potential contribution to improving the quality of tourism education. The findings highlight the importance of integrating innovative digital technologies into educational practices to prepare future tourism professionals for the changing demands of the tourism industry.

Fragmented data architectures may limit how artificial intelligence (AI)-based digital mental health systems combine and communicate multimodal information. This scenario-based study tested whether users perceived the Integrated framework more favorably than the Traditional framework. U.S. adults familiar with digital mental health technologies reviewed standardized descriptions of both conditions and rated system quality, information quality, and perceived transparency and explainability. The constructs covered data quality, portability, response time, accuracy, timeliness, completeness, transparency, and explainability. Paired-samples t tests were supplemented by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Valid paired samples were 277, 267, and 258 for the three constructs, respectively. Ratings favored the Integrated condition for system quality (M = 3.47 vs. 3.38; t (276) = −2.66, P = 0.008, |dz| = 0.16), information quality (M = 3.48 vs. 3.34; t (266) = −4.49, P dz| = 0.28), and perceived transparency and explainability (M = 3.79 vs. 3.65; t (257) = −3.04, P = 0.003, |dz| = 0.19). Nonparametric analyses supported the same conclusions. Absolute paired effect magnitudes ranged from |dz| = 0.16 to |dz| = 0.28. Because participants evaluated descriptions rather than functioning systems and temporal alignment was bundled with integration, the findings identify a modest perceptual advantage rather than causal, technical, or clinical-performance benefits. The results support further user-centered prototype and implementation testing.

This study compares the private and public education sectors using a quantitative survey approach to examine the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English teaching among 189 secondary school teachers in Iraq. Significant sector differences are revealed by the results, which show that private school teachers were more aware of AI, had better facilities, and used it more in the classroom. Inadequate teacher training (84.1%), deficiencies in tech infrastructure (78.3%), financial limitations (71.4%), a lack of institutional support (69.3%), and teacher opposition to change (63.0%) are the main obstacles to implementation. However, educators in both fields demonstrated favorable opinions regarding AI, acknowledging its benefits for improving student engagement, personalizing instruction, giving instant feedback, and fostering the development of 21st-century abilities. The study recommends infrastructure improvement, equal resource distribution to public schools, structured teacher training, and supportive rules and regulations to enable successful AI application.

Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now entering radiology, where they can analyze imaging data quantitatively and lessen dependence on subjective visual reading. This study investigated the perceived impact of AI implementation on radiology workflows and the professional roles of radiologists in the radiology department at King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC), Saudi Arabia. Methods: This study used a cross-sectional design at KAMC in Saudi Arabia. An online questionnaire was distributed to radiologists working at KAMC locations in Jeddah, Riyadh, and Al-Ahsa. A total of 100 participants responded. Demographic data, including gender, age, department, and professional rank, were collected and analyzed in Microsoft Excel and R version 4.2.2 (31 October 2022; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) in RStudio version 2026.01.1+403 (Posit PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Results: 81% of participants agreed or strongly agreed that AI would reduce time and improve healthcare, and 82% that it could improve image interpretation and reduce false-positive and false-negative errors. In addition, 69% agreed or strongly agreed that AI may reduce radiologists’ workload, and 56% that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages. However, 38% agreed that AI may reduce radiologists’ job opportunities, 33% were concerned about possible loss of patient data, and only 43% would trust AI to make an accurate diagnosis. No significant differences were found by gender or professional rank; across departments, only the perception that AI’s advantages outweigh its disadvantages differed significantly (p = 0.004), with interventional radiologists agreeing less than pediatric and cardiovascular radiologists. Conclusions: AI was generally viewed positively by radiologists, although notable concerns regarding data security, diagnostic trust, and job opportunities were also identified. AI was perceived as having the potential to improve workflow and reduce workload. Although AI may change the roles of radiologists, it is not expected to replace them entirely. Instead, it is likely to shift their responsibilities while helping reduce their workload. These findings are consistent with previous research and highlight AI’s potential to support healthcare professionals in delivering faster, more accurate, and more effective diagnostic services.

documents.abstract: The article analyzes the relationship between personality and emotional willpower from a scientific and psychological perspective. Emotional willpower is interpreted as an individual’s ability to recognize and regulate emotional states, suppress impulsive tendencies, and overcome difficulties in achieving long-term goals. Drawing on classical (Vygotsky, Leontiev) and contemporary approaches (emotional intelligence, self-determination theory, and the Big Five model), the article explores the cognitive, motivational, and neuropsychological mechanisms underlying emotional willpower. The structure of personality, intrinsic motivation, emotional regulation, and developmental patterns throughout ontogenesis are examined in an interconnected manner. Practical approaches to developing emotional willpower are presented, and its significance for personal integration, stress resilience, and social adaptation is substantiated.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is widely credited with enabling personalized learning, yet evidence on how AI-driven personalization functions in low-resource, multilingual African classrooms remains scarce. This study examined how the integration of AI affects personalized learning outcomes at Discovery School, a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi. A convergent mixed-methods design combined a structured survey (n = 110: administrators, teachers, students, parents) with semi-structured interviews (n = 35), analyzed respectively in SPSS 27 (descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression) and NVivo 14 (six-phase thematic analysis, Cohen's κ = 0.83), and triangulated using a joint-display approach. The analysis was guided by Constructivist Learning Theory (CLT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Stakeholders reported high perceived AI effectiveness for personalized learning (M = 3.98, SD = 0.71), and students strongly valued the ability to learn at their own pace (M = 4.34, SD = 0.58; 89% agreement). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and student engagement were strongly and significantly correlated (r = 0.74-0.82, p < .01). Multiple regression showed that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, motivation, and infrastructure reliability jointly explained 46% of the variance in self-reported academic improvement (R² = 0.46), with perceived usefulness the strongest individual predictor (β = 0.42, p < .001). However, gains in engagement were not matched by corresponding gains in standardized test performance, revealing a perception-performance gap. Qualitative data showed teachers using AI dashboards diagnostically to scaffold instruction within students’ zones of proximal development, and students describing genuine, if algorithmically bounded, autonomy over pace and repetition. The study proposes two theoretical extensions — data-mediated constructivism and bounded autonomy — and concludes that AI functions as a pedagogical enhancer whose benefits are real but conditional on teacher capacity, infrastructure reliability, and equitable access, since 12.7% of respondents reported no reliable technology access outside school.

documents.abstract: Despite the growing interest in integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language teaching, limited research has examined the opportunities AI could provide for activity adaptations in English coursebooks. Through an exploratory qualitative design, this study aimed to reveal AI-supported adaptation suggestions from 25 pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers. It asked two questions: what activity adaptations for language skills are suggested and at which level the suggested adaptations in the Substitution-Augmentation-Modification-Redefinition (SAMR) framework are. The participants adapted one skill activity using AI and explained and justified their adaptations in written reports. The inductive thematic analysis of the reports revealed 19 adaptation suggestions, ten of which were in the transformation category and nine could serve as enhancements for traditional education practices according to the SAMR framework. Speaking was the skill with the highest number of suggested adaptations, followed by reading, writing, and listening skills. The common adaptation patterns among skills were AI as background knowledge supporter, AI as multicultural awareness builder, multimodal artefacts generator, and AI as a chatbot for oral and written practice. The study may contribute to discussions on AI supported materials development in EFL and teacher education fields by illustrating pre-service teachers’ conceptualizations of AI-supported coursebook activity adaptations and a critical evaluation of the suggestions through the SAMR.

The use of Artificial Intelligence in teacher education is seen as having great potential. AI tools can help alleviate teachers’ workloads and support learners individually. However, they are still relatively rarely used by practicing teachers and currently, there is a lack of empirical findings regarding the use of AI tools and the factors influencing AI usage behavior among pre-service teachers. Following Taylor and Todd (1995) by extending the Theory of Planned Behavior with the Technology Acceptance Model, this study investigates factors that influence pre-service teachers’ weekly use of AI. In an empirical-quantitative study, N = 931 pre-service teachers across Germany were asked about their perceived usefulness, subjective norm, self-efficacy beliefs, and behavioral intention to use AI tools in their future teaching practice. They also provided information about their average weekly AI usage time. The results of a structural equation model indicate that the behavioral intention to use AI tools in the future is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norm, and participants’ self-efficacy beliefs. Additionally, behavioral intention and self-efficacy beliefs are significantly linked with the weekly duration of AI use. Specifically, the association between pre-service teachers‘ self-efficacy beliefs and weekly AI use was partly accounted for statistically by behavioral intention. The results provide important insights into how to promote the use of AI tools in teacher education.

BACKGROUND: Machine-learning-based clinical decision support is entering routine care, but its value depends on whether clinicians can judge when to follow its advice and when to override it. Evidence suggests this judgment is often poorly calibrated in both directions. Whether displaying a model's predictive uncertainty helps physicians integrate advice more selectively is unclear. METHODS: In a preregistered, randomized vignette experiment, 227 physicians produced 1,802 sepsis risk assessments. Physicians gave an initial risk estimate, saw advice from a machine-learning system, and revised their estimate. They were randomized to see a risk score alone, or the score together with one of two visual representations of predictive uncertainty: icon arrays with uncertainty bands, or quantile dotplots. Outcomes were advice uptake, accuracy of the revised risk estimate, and trust. RESULTS: Here we show that both uncertainty representations increase advice uptake relative to the risk score alone, by 23% and 21%, and that the gap between correct and incorrect advice is descriptively about twice as large. Uptake of incorrect advice is not reliably reduced. Both formats improve the accuracy of revised risk estimates, with the larger effect for quantile dotplots, but only icon arrays increase trust. Physicians describe uncertainty as actionable only where they can tell why it is elevated. CONCLUSIONS: Displaying predictive uncertainty changes how physicians integrate machine-learning advice, but the representation format determines whether the benefit appears mainly as accuracy or trust. The effect is partial: uncertainty representations support recognizing reliable advice more than rejecting unreliable advice.

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE To systematically review and quantitatively synthesize the evidence on the predictors of the use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health support. METHOD We searched PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, for quantitative studies that examined factors associated with the use of AI chatbots for mental health support. We assessed the methodological quality of the studies with the revised Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool for analytical cross-sectional studies. We pooled adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with random-effects models for predictors that had been examined in at least three studies, and we performed several sensitivity analyses. RESULTS We included eight cross-sectional studies with 7864 participants from the United States, Greece and Canada. Mental health service use (pooled OR = 1.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.33 to 1.98), depressive symptoms (pooled OR = 1.65, 95% CI = 1.38 to 1.98) and Asian race (pooled OR = 1.87, 95% CI = 1.46 to 2.41) were associated with higher odds of AI chatbot use for mental health support, and these associations were robust in all sensitivity analyses. Anxiety symptoms, younger age and Hispanic ethnicity were also associated with higher odds of use, although these associations were not robust in sensitivity analyses. Sex, suicidality and Black race were not associated with use, while the frequency of use among users was not associated with sex or mental health service use. CONCLUSIONS Individuals who already use mental health services and those with depressive symptoms are more likely to use AI chatbots for mental health support, which suggests that these tools may be used alongside, rather than instead of, professional care.

documents.abstract: Introduction: Burnout syndrome represented a relevant occupational health problem among nursing staff due to constant exposure to physical, emotional, and organizational demands. The objective was to analyze its prevalence in hospital institutions and identify the main occupational, personal, and organizational factors associated with its occurrence. Methodology: A narrative search of scientific literature was conducted in biomedical and nursing databases, emphasizing recent publications and systematic reviews addressing prevalence, associated factors, and consequences of burnout. The evidence reviewed showed variations in prevalence estimates according to populations, hospital services, measurement instruments, and work contexts. A review published in 2025 identified global prevalence rates of 33.45% for emotional exhaustion, 25.0% for depersonalization, and 33.49% for low personal accomplishment. Results: The main associated factors were work overload, long working hours, shift work, time pressure, lack of organizational support, role conflicts, and occupational stress. Greater vulnerability was identified in high-demand areas, such as emergency departments and intensive care units. Burnout was also associated with physical and mental health problems, absenteeism, staff turnover, and reduced quality and safety of patient care. Conclusions: Burnout syndrome constituted a multifactorial problem that affected nursing staff well-being and the quality of hospital services. Prevention and early detection, together with improvements in working conditions, shift organization, communication, and institutional support, were considered essential to reducing associated factors and promoting safe patient care.

Cognitive engagement shapes learning but resists direct observation, and the spread of generative-AI chatbots in EFL writing has made post hoc self-reports even harder to trust. This study asks whether the depth of a learner’s prompts (their specificity, elaboration, metacognitive framing, higher-order quality, and iterative refinement) can serve as a behavioural trace of that engagement. Using the RECIPE4U dataset (1,913 prompts from 130 EFL learners), two coders scored three prompt-level dimensions with substantial to near-perfect agreement (κ = .74–.84); the remaining dimensions were derived from intent annotations and session structure. The five dimensions did not behave as one construct. At the student level, only elaboration correlated with essay revision (r = .34) and, weakly, with satisfaction (r = .20); metacognitive framing and higher-order request added little, and iterative refinement related negatively to revision (r = −.18). An equal-weight composite showed no association with either criterion (r = .07). Each one-point increase in prompting depth was associated with more than twice the odds of subsequent revision (OR = 2.37; course-adjusted OR = 2.09), an association that persisted in a random-intercept model despite marked between-student variance (ICC = .41). Prompting depth is best read dimension by dimension: elaboration, not depth in the aggregate, tracks revision-oriented engagement.

documents.abstract: The increasing automation of nuclear power plants introduces novel demands on operator situation awareness and workload management. Yet, commonly used measures of situation awareness and workload often lack comprehensive validation within nuclear contexts. This study evaluates four prominent measures: two of situation awareness (3D SART and SACRI) and two of workload (NASA-TLX and a secondary task performance metric) according to key psychometric criteria for nuclear control room simulations. Using the Rancor Microworld platform, twenty-six participants completed both routine and abnormal scenarios under different automation levels, following a within-subjects design. SACRI correlated with generated revenue and task time, NASA-TLX correlated with temperature management and number of actions, and secondary task performance correlated with task time; 3D SART showed no correlations. Predictive analyses showed that these relationships largely disappeared when automation level and scenario type were included as covariates. Sensitivity to experimental conditions varied across measures, with 3D SART and NASA-TLX affected by automation level, and NASA-TLX, SACRI and secondary task performance by scenario type. Measures were not redundant, and all demonstrated moderate reliability across experimental conditions. Findings provide insight to researchers and nuclear practitioners for selecting situation awareness and workload assessment tools and strengthening the technical basis for designing safer and more effective control room systems.

O estresse ocupacional e a qualidade de vida no trabalho constituem aspectos relevantes para a saúde dos Agentes Comunitários de Saúde (ACS) e para a organização da Atenção Primária à Saúde. Este estudo observacional, de abordagem quantitativa e delineamento transversal, descritivo e correlacional, teve como objetivo analisar esses constructos entre ACS do município de Santa Luzia, Paraíba, e investigar a associação entre eles. A pesquisa contou com 35 participantes, que responderam a um questionário sociodemográfico e profissional, a um instrumento de qualidade de vida no trabalho fundamentado no modelo de Walton e à Escala de Estresse no Trabalho. Os dados foram analisados por meio de estatística descritiva e correlação de Spearman. Os resultados evidenciaram nível elevado de estresse ocupacional e avaliação desfavorável da qualidade de vida no trabalho, com médias de 3,84 e 2,38, respectivamente. Identificou-se associação negativa e estatisticamente significativa entre os constructos, especialmente nas dimensões condições de trabalho e trabalho e espaço total de vida. Conclui-se que melhores condições laborais e maior equilíbrio entre trabalho e vida pessoal são aspectos importantes para a qualidade de vida dos ACS, destacando-se a necessidade de ações institucionais voltadas à valorização profissional, ao suporte organizacional e à promoção de ambientes de trabalho saudáveis.

documents.abstract: Large language models are approaching general-purpose capability, yet three failure modes—hallucination, ethical misalignment, and cognitive rigidity—continue to block reliable deployment, and existing defenses address them only reactively at the output level. This paper presents the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a cognitive-safety infrastructure that treats contradiction as a source of negative entropy and organizes defense as a five-stage closed loop: definition, adversarial engagement, iterative verification, convergence, and ethical fusing. RAE formulates model self-correction as a recursive fixed-point problem, quantifies cognitive quality through topological metrics, distributes adversarial pressure across a pool of heterogeneous agents, and enforces ethical boundaries through dual-layer circuit breakers. A system specification and internal deployment observations indicate that the design targets self-referential vulnerability false-alarm rates below 1%, consensus variance at or above ln(2), and parallel adversarial pools exceeding 100 agents. We compare RAE with conventional filtering, instruction tuning, and static red teaming, and discuss the framework's theoretical status, evaluation limitations, and deployment requirements for high-stakes domains.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming classroom teaching, yet two-wave repeated cross-sectional evidence on how K-12 teachers develop the knowledge that underpins intelligent performance with AI remains scarce. Our two-year study across 29 schools thus explored the associations between university-facilitated teacher action research and the development of artificial intelligence technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK), a domain-specific form of intelligence-as-knowledge in teaching. Data were collected using questionnaires on research-related dispositions and AI-TPACK with 285 participants in Year 1 and 200 participants in Year 2. Structural equation modeling suggested that the associations of teachers’ research consumption and production with their AI-TPACK differed between the two waves, possibly reflecting shifting program task requirements, whereas research attitude served as a stable predictor. The findings yield preliminary evidence regarding linkages between action research and teachers’ AI-TPACK, and highlight the differences in these associations across the two waves. Considered from the perspective of adult intellectual development, these results suggest that knowledge in professional practice might be sustained by opportunities to convert inquiry into produced knowledge, refining accounts of how expertise with intelligent technologies develops.

Academic dishonesty has long been a concern in computing education, and the rapid growth of online learning and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has further complicated how cheating is perceived and addressed. We report on a study examining how different actors in the computer science (CS) classroom interpret potential cheating scenarios and the motivations behind academic dishonesty. Participants included instructors (n = 6), teaching assistants (TAs; n = 22), and undergraduate students (n = 538) enrolled in two CS courses at a large Southeastern institution in the United States. Respondents classified scenarios as serious cheating, trivial cheating, or not cheating and responded to an open-ended question about motivations for academic dishonesty. Our findings reveal differences in perceptions across the three stakeholder groups. Among the instructors who participated, grade pressure and laziness were the most frequently mentioned motivations for academic dishonesty, whereas students and TAs more frequently emphasized gaps in prerequisite knowledge and time management challenges. Given the small instructor sample, these qualitative findings should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than representative of instructors more broadly. These results highlight differences in how academic dishonesty is understood across classroom stakeholders and underscore the need for clearer communication of academic-integrity expectations and instructional strategies that help students interpret and navigate those expectations in computing education, particularly in post-COVID learning environments where hybrid instruction, increased reliance on digital resources, and AI-assisted tools have reshaped students’ approaches to coursework and learning.

In shared control and shared autonomy (SC/SA) systems, humans collaborate with robot agents to achieve common goals. Such systems enable collaborations beyond what either agent could do alone, benefiting from the relative strengths of humans (e.g., reasoning, planning) and robots (e.g., precision, repeatability). Research in this area dates back over 40 years, with numerous applications, such as in manufacturing, robot-assisted surgery, and assistive technologies. Shared control approaches have even seen some large-scale commercialization efforts in areas like semi-autonomous driving and automotive assembly. Without SC/SA, we may not have seen robots deployed in settings where manual teleoperation alone is too difficult, such as delicate laparoscopic surgical procedures or the remote operation of space manipulators. Recently, SC/SA approaches have gained significant traction, with hundreds of new methods published in scientific papers each year. In this paper, we examine recent approaches and trends in these methods, investigating several crucial aspects that are underexplored in previous surveys. We reviewed 195 papers across a 5-year time window (2020 to 2024) in three high-impact robotics venues (IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, and Science Robotics). First, we provide descriptive statistics and trends related to human input methods, technical approaches, and applications. Second, we provide a perspective on the growing role of generative artificial intelligence approaches in SC/SA. Based on these insights, we offer updated recommendations for future approaches.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools now write, explain, and debug code, which changes how computing students learn and how their work is assessed. Instructors, however, act within institutional guidance written largely with essays in mind. We report a document analysis of the public, institution-level GenAI guidance of the 13 members of Polytechnics Canada and the 15 members of the U15 Group of Canadian Research Universities, retrieved in October 2026. Using a 27-item codebook spanning governance, integrity and assessment, data and legal issues, values, AI literacy, and a computing lens, we find that both sectors leave course-level decisions to instructors, although polytechnics more often prohibit use unless the instructor permits it (8 of 13 vs. 4 of 14), and converge on disclosure, links to academic integrity policy, and, in most institutions, the expectation that programs adapt rules to their discipline. Polytechnics frame GenAI as workforce preparation substantively far more often (7 of 13 vs. 0 of 14), whereas universities more often address assessment redesign. Twelve of 27 institutions with retrievable guidance mention code, but almost always as one output type among many; none names an AI coding assistant or provides substantive code-specific guidance on attribution, assessment, or licensing. Institution-level guidance is thus not silent on code but leaves programming-specific questions largely to programs and instructors. We propose five elements of discipline-level guidance for computing and release our codebook and coded dataset.

Existing discussions of ethical AI often move between normative principles and localized accounts of ethical practice. We argue that these two orientations should not be treated as separate or competing. Normative values such as fairness, autonomy, and accountability must be examined in relation to how specific sociotechnical arrangements reproduce or intensify concrete injustices for differently positioned language users. Drawing on complementary scholarship in applied linguistics and philosophy, this article analyzes two sites of ethical tension: AI assessment systems and AI‐assisted language learning. In AI assessment, we show how fairness must account for how AI impacts assessment constructs and whether assessment judgments are answerable to learners. In AI‐assisted learning, we show how datafied personalization and algorithmic preemption reshape learner autonomy and language learning processes. Building on these analyses, we propose three directions for ethical AI in applied linguistics: moving toward the justice of AI‐mediated language practices, toward a relational understanding of learner autonomy, and toward AI ethics as pedagogy. We contend that ethical AI requires an ongoing responsibility to preserve language users’ space to negotiate AI in ways that expand rather than narrow their multilingual meaning‐making resources and communicative possibilities.

documents.abstract: Developers increasingly act as managers of AI agents: they hand tasks to AI coding agents and then have to understand, verify, ship, and learn from what the agents produce. IDEs and recent tools can show which committed lines were written by AI, but they do not attribute the pending changes of external agents, and they do not use attribution to help the developer review, learn, or judge risk. We present SmartLens, an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that attributes changes to an AI agent, the developer, or both. It combines this attribution with the Git history to support three goals: (i) Learn compares the skills (APIs, language features, annotations) that agents used with the skills the developer has used in their own commits; (ii) Understand ranks pending changes by review priority; and (iii) Risk shows hotspots: files that change often, are mostly written by AI, and that the developer barely knows. In a preliminary evaluation, SmartLens attributed 8 of 12 scripted IDE scenarios correctly; all failures were in (expected) blind spots. On 8 Open Source Software repositories with agent co-authored commits, agents introduced up to 253 skills that do not appear in the main developer's own commits. The Risk ranking was as good as or better than plain churn at predicting later bug fixes, but part of this gain is due to recency.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a source of social influence. But people often prefer human over AI sources (algorithm aversion/preference for humans), which might prevent AI from influencing humans. However, we outline a theoretical framework that suggests that preferences do not play a causal role in influence. To test this framework, we investigated under which conditions preferences predict AI influence. Participants (N = 1,254) indicated their adviser preference and then made incentivised decisions while receiving advice from AI or human advisers. Participants preferred human over AI advisers but were influenced by AI and humans similarly. A strong aversion to AI advisers had no (Study 1) or a trivial relation (Study 2 and 3) with AI influence, which was explained by confounding variables. When manipulated, preferences did not predict advice-taking, but adviser trustworthiness and competence did (Study 3). Our results suggest that for predicting AI influence, understanding domain-specific social cognitions, not preferences, is critical.

documents.abstract: This article in the journal Gruppe. Interaktion. Organisation. (GIO) examines how organizations can intentionally develop, maintain, and continuously adapt shared mental models (SMMs) across team, functional, and hierarchical boundaries. Whereas prior research has primarily investigated the characteristics, measurement, and effects of SMMs within teams, comparatively less is known about how shared cognitive orientations emerge and can be cultivated within heterogeneous organizational and socio-technological networks. This question is particularly relevant to socio-technological transformation and human-AI collaboration, where divergent professional perspectives, technological systems, and evolving task allocations intensify the need for cognitive alignment. Based on a structured narrative literature review, the paper conceptualizes SMMs as boundary spanning cognitive infrastructures and derives overarching enabling conditions and five principles for their development and maintenance. Leadership, organizational culture, and psychological safety provide the necessary enabling conditions. Joint situational analysis, visual and scenario-based co-construction, and interdisciplinary skill profiles and shared language support SMM development. Iterative feedback loops and the deliberate unlearning of outdated assumptions enable their continuous adaptation. Actor-Network Theory complements this perspective by explaining how shared understandings emerge through translation, are mediated by material and digital artefacts, and become stabilized within socio-technical networks. The paper thereby extends SMM research toward an organization-wide and process-oriented perspective and provides actionable guidance for managing socio-technological transformation.

documents.abstract: Perkembangan kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan transformasi digital telah membawa perubahan dalam penyelenggaraan pendidikan serta membuka peluang untuk menciptakan pembelajaran yang lebih adaptif dan inovatif. Namun, pemanfaatan teknologi dalam pendidikan perlu diintegrasikan dengan prinsip pembangunan berkelanjutan agar mampu mendukung pengembangan kompetensi generasi muda yang memiliki kepedulian terhadap lingkungan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis strategi inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan berbasis kecerdasan buatan dan transformasi digital dalam membangun kompetensi generasi muda berwawasan lingkungan. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dengan pendekatan deskriptif kualitatif. Pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui penelusuran, pemilihan, dan pengkajian artikel jurnal ilmiah yang relevan, kemudian dianalisis melalui tahapan identifikasi, pengelompokan, perbandingan, dan sintesis temuan berdasarkan fokus penelitian. Hasil kajian menunjukkan enam aspek utama dalam inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan, yaitu transformasi digital sebagai fondasi pembelajaran adaptif, pemanfaatan AI untuk mendukung personalisasi dan efisiensi pembelajaran, penguatan kompetensi pendidik, integrasi Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), penerapan pembelajaran kontekstual berbasis Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) dan Project-Based Learning (PjBL), serta pengembangan kompetensi generasi muda. Hasil kajian juga menunjukkan bahwa penggunaan AI secara berlebihan berpotensi mengurangi keterlibatan peserta didik dalam proses berpikir sehingga diperlukan penguatan literasi digital dan kemampuan berpikir kritis. Dengan demikian, inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan perlu mengintegrasikan teknologi, kompetensi pendidik, dan pendekatan pembelajaran yang berorientasi pada keberlanjutan untuk mendukung terbentuknya generasi muda yang kritis, kreatif, adaptif, serta memiliki literasi dan kepedulian lingkungan.

documents.abstract: This repository presents the consolidated research corpus of Structural Intelligence (SI), an interdisciplinary theoretical framework developed by Vladisav Jovanović within the broader research program of the Philosophy of Structure. The collection reorganizes 27 original publications into seven integrated manuscripts: Coherence, Contact, and Answerability; The Architecture of Correction; Evidence-Constrained Interpretation; Structural Debt; Structural Capture; Organization and Adaptation; and Wisdom Under Pressure. Together, these manuscripts examine the relationships between coherence, evidence, warranted correction, adaptive organization, human agency, and the distribution of unresolved costs. They situate the framework in relation to established research in epistemology, cognitive psychology, cybernetics, systems theory, enactivism, organizational learning, resilience engineering, and artificial intelligence evaluation. Structural Intelligence is presented as an integrative conceptual framework with testable research hypotheses, rather than a universal causal theory or a validated psychometric construct. The repository preserves the original manuscripts, revised consolidated publications, source inventories, content-preservation documentation, and SHA-256 checksums. Editable manuscript sources and supporting materials are included where available. Its purpose is to reduce bibliographic fragmentation while preserving the intellectual development, provenance, and conceptual contributions of the original research. The collection provides a coherent foundation for subsequent theoretical development, independent evaluation, and empirical investigation.

Gratitude writing can support well-being, but independent practice may lack guidance. Generative AI could help while shaping reflection, agency, and ownership. We investigated how gratitude-writing format and AI-assistance mode influence well-being and writing experiences. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (N=401), participants completed a gratitude reflection or a gratitude letter using two AI-assistance modes: scaffolding, which provided reflective questions after inactivity, or co-writing, which offered inline text suggestions. Participants' well-being improved after using our AI-assisted gratitude-writing system, consistent with the activity's intended benefits. However, participants' experiences revealed a trade-off between the AI-support types: co-writing received higher usability ratings, yet its immediacy could disrupt writing, and greater suggestion acceptance was associated with weaker perceived agency. Scaffolding supported stronger perceived human ownership but was sometimes overlooked. These findings extend human-AI writing research beyond productivity and text quality by showing how AI involvement shapes psychological outcomes and the experience of self-guided, emotionally meaningful writing.

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased interest in understanding individuals’ intention to use AI. However, little is known about how this intention is related to entrepreneurial alertness (EA) and entrepreneurial intention (EI). This study examined the relationships among behavioral intention to use AI (BI-AI), EA, and EI among university students in Türkiye. It also explored whether trait competitiveness (TC) and family entrepreneurial background (FB) moderate the relationship between EA and EI. Data were collected from 355 participants through an online cross-sectional survey. The measurement model was evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis together with reliability and validity assessments. PROCESS macro analyses with bootstrap confidence intervals were then used to test the proposed direct, indirect, and moderating relationships. The results showed that BI-AI was positively related to EA (b = 0.111, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [0.054, 0.167]). However, no significant direct relationship was found between BI-AI and EI (b = −0.017, SE = 0.078, 95% CI [−0.170, 0.135]. EA was positively related to EI (b = 1.136, SE = 0.142, 95% CI [0.857, 1.414]). The indirect relationship between BI-AI and EI through EA was also significant (b = 0.126, SE = 0.060, 95% CI [0.026, 0.256]). In the moderation analysis (N = 351), trait competitiveness significantly moderated the relationship between EA and EI (b = 0.231, SE = 0.060, 95% CI [0.113, 0.348]). Family entrepreneurial background, however, did not significantly moderate this relationship (b = −0.203, SE = 0.140, 95% CI [−0.478, 0.073]). The data indicate that EA may be relevant to understanding the link between BI-AI and EI and that the association between EA and EI is stronger among those with higher levels of TC. Because the study relied on cross-sectional data, the results should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than proof that one condition causes another. Future longitudinal and intervention-based research may provide a better understanding of how BI-AI, EA, and EI evolve over time.

As artificial intelligence (AI) automates work for which established methods of problem formulation and solution already exist, the ability to act where such methods do not yet exist or no longer apply becomes relatively more valuable. This paper examines a cognitive dimension of complexity arising from the relationship between the properties of the reality under investigation and the cognitive capabilities of the subject (an individual or a team). Even before a problem is explicitly formulated, the language used to describe a real situation can introduce distortions. Three types of difficulty are distinguished by what must change: the model, the problem space, or the cognitive capabilities of the subject. AI can reinforce existing limitations as well as help reveal them; the outcome depends on how human–AI interaction is organized. The paper outlines a research agenda for Complexity Lab in which interaction with reality under incomplete knowledge may itself become a mechanism of cognitive development. It is addressed to leaders in business, engineering, and applied science.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in collective decision-making, people's perceptions of AI may shape who reaches agreement and what they receive. We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.

documents.abstract: Play represents an important factor in the learning process and the development of children's personalities, particularly when it is purposefully used as a means of achieving educational objectives. Contemporary educational approaches increasingly emphasize teaching practices that encourage students' active participation, intrinsic motivation, creativity and independent learning. In this context, the concept of “Learning through Play” represents an important foundation for reconsidering traditional teaching practices and the possibilities of integrating play into contemporary education. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the pedagogical significance of didactic games, with particular reference to the UNESCO report “Why the World Needs Happy Schools: Global Report on Happiness in and for Learning” (2024). The aim is to examine the relationship between learning through play, active student participation, motivation and the creation of a supportive learning environment. The paper applies a qualitative theoretical and analytical approach based on content analysis of the document and interpretation of relevant scientific research. Particular attention is given to the teacher's role in planning and guiding play-based activities, as well as to the conditions under which didactic games can contribute to meaningful and quality learning. The paper concludes that didactic games should not be understood merely as additional or entertaining activities, but as a pedagogically designed approach that connects knowledge with experience, activity and students' personal engagement.

documents.abstract: AI chatbots are making their way into ecommerce as "24/7" on-demand interfaces to guide, resolve, and inquiry. However, its implementation does not promise a better experience or increased brand attachment. We theorize from available research about chatbot property-construals on consumers' experience and satisfaction, and how those experiences lead to retention, repurchase and loyalty. A structured integrative review of peer reviewed empirical articles and reviews, derived mainly from 2020 to November 2026, and the extant literature on customer experience, information-systems success and expectation-confirmation was conducted in which publications were analyzed via thematic comparisons and a study-level matrix; no primary data, pooled effects, or statistical models were studied. Consistently, responsiveness, informational quality, relevance, reliability and service recovery lead to positive end-states; empathy and social presence foster trust, and social cues (such as humanlike appearance) may do so as well. Meta-analyses show that chatbot satisfaction is positively correlated with behavioral intentions but that the relatively large between-studies heterogeneity tempers the generality of these findings. Research in other industries shows that although chatbots can grab consumers' attention, its effects on emotional stimulation are uncertain and technology-induced errors cause cognitive dissonance, with accompanying frustration and reduced service quality ratings. We conclude with an integrative journey framework involving interaction personality-construals, experience, satisfaction and outcomes. Chatbots will be most effective at engendering loyalty if they guide consumers accurately, effectively and with good timing, manage their own capabilities and provide quick escalation procedures when conditions demand.

This exploratory study illuminates the “black box” of student reasoning by examining how information systems students engaged with generative AI tools (ChatGPT) during a complex SQL exam. Using qualitative thematic analysis of 33 interaction transcripts, we identified preliminary behavioral patterns that differentiate successful from unsuccessful problem-solving. In this sense, these interactions resemble a digital think-aloud, in which AI transcripts provide insights into the internal thought processes associated with problem-solving. Analysis suggests a spectrum of interactions from “Strategic AI Engagement” (the “pilot”) to “Procedural AI Dependency” (the “passenger”). Successful engagements appeared to involve iterative refinement, systematic validation, and adaptive strategy shifts. Conversely, unsuccessful interactions tended to reflect a conceptual bypass characterized by passive query reception, rigid approaches, and an abdication of technical reasoning to the AI. The findings suggest that as technical proficiency shifts from procedural code generation toward evaluative judgment, educators should design AI-assisted assignments that prioritize auditing, verification, and strategic questioning. More broadly, the study suggests that GenAI can support but not replace the foundational competence and reflective judgment essential for effective problem-solving in data-driven professional environments.

documents.abstract: This multidisciplinary perspective paper examines the rise of artificial intelligence, robotics and automation and their potential effects on human employment and livelihood. The paper considers technological progress from economic, psychological, social, philosophical, ethical and religious perspectives. It explores how automation may transform employment in hospitality, manufacturing, transportation, retail, administrative work and other sectors while also considering the new forms of employment that technological development may create. Particular attention is given to the human consequences of involuntary job displacement, including financial insecurity, identity, dignity, psychological wellbeing and economic inequality. The paper also examines the responsibilities of technology developers, employers, governments, workers and consumers during periods of technological transition. A distinctive part of the discussion considers Islamic concepts of justice, Rizq, human responsibility and the supplication of the oppressed in relation to technological displacement. This religious discussion is presented as ethical analysis and does not constitute a formal Islamic legal ruling or fatwa. The paper ultimately argues for human centred automation, in which technological progress is evaluated not only by efficiency and productivity but also by its contribution to human dignity, security and wellbeing. This is a perspective paper based on secondary research and personal interpretation. It does not present original experimental or survey data.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important component of modern education, particularly in the field of English language teaching. The integration of AI-powered educational technologies creates new opportunities for improving language acquisition, developing communicative competence, and providing individualized learning experiences. This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, focusing on its potential to enhance the four fundamental language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. The study explores the pedagogical advantages of AI-based tools, including personalized instruction, automated feedback, adaptive learning, and increased learner motivation. Furthermore, it considers the challenges associated with AI integration, such as technological dependence, limited digital literacy, data privacy, and the importance of maintaining the teacher's professional role. The article emphasizes that artificial intelligence should be regarded as a supportive educational instrument rather than a replacement for human teachers. The effective implementation of AI requires a balanced approach that combines technological innovation with pedagogical principles and learner-centred instruction.

Multidisciplinary tumor boards (MTBs) are the gold standard for breast cancer (BC) treatment planning, but rising caseloads and the growing number of clinical, pathological, and molecular factors under consideration are straining their capacity. AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), has been proposed as a decision support tool, and BC is the tumor type for which AI-MTB concordance has been studied most. We conducted a narrative critical review of studies comparing AI-generated treatment recommendations with breast MTB recommendations, along with evidence on MTB performance, earlier rule-based decision support systems, and the relevant regulatory and medico-legal environment. We evaluated 17 LLM studies published between 2023 and 2026. Overall concordance ranged from 16% to 94%, increasing with model generation, structured input, and guideline grounding, and decreasing with disease stage and case complexity. Concordance was consistently high for endocrine therapy and standard indications for systemic therapy, variable for surgery, radiotherapy, and genomic testing, and low or inconsistent for genetic counseling, anti-HER2 regimen selection, and the management of metastatic disease. Reproducibility was poor, and no study examined patient outcomes. Concordance with the MTB is not equivalent to clinical correctness, and hallucinations, the handling of incomplete information, and automation bias are distinct safety dimensions that concordance does not capture; we therefore propose a multidimensional evaluation framework. The current, limited evidence base supports using AI as a supervised, guideline-grounded pre-MTB tool in treatment planning rather than as a replacement for the MTB itself.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

documents.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how the explanation depth and conversational naturalness of generative AI (GenAI) stock assistants relate to retail investors' perceived epistemic trust, perceived control, continuance intention and self-reported value co-creation, and how hallucination risk, overload and literacy condition these associations. Design/methodology/approach – Drawing on cognitive appraisal and epistemic trust theories, a cross-sectional survey of 386 Indonesian retail investors was analyzed with PLS-SEM, Gaussian copulas, PLSpredict, CVPAT and importance–performance map analysis (IPMA). Findings – Both design features were positively associated with trust and control, which were associated with continuance and co-creation. Perceived hallucination risk strengthened the explanation depth–trust association but weakened the naturalness–trust association. Overload was negatively related to control without significantly moderating the design features. Literacy moderated the trust–outcome associations in opposite directions. The explanation depth–control path was not robust to endogeneity correction. Research limitations/implications – The cross-sectional, self-reported, single-country design precludes causal inference; trust calibration against actual AI accuracy was not assessed. Practical implications – Providers could prioritize verifiable, layered explanations over conversational polish; regulators could consider disclosure and verification-literacy guidance. Originality/value – The study introduces perceived stock data hallucination risk as a context-specific construct and links perceived trust and self-reported engagement to managerial priorities.

BACKGROUND: I chronicle a new, unique paradigm shift at the intersection of human creativity and generative artificial intelligence. Following my retirement, I engaged the large language model Google Gemini as a digital co-pilot for my administrative and scientific activities. CASE STUDY: What began as a tool for basic text formatting, rapidly evolved into a sophisticated, synergistic collaboration, culminating in the co-authorship of a quantitative scientific manuscript in the field of "cultural musicology", a totally new field of investigation for me. AI ADVANTAGES: Based on my experience, I explore the profound structural advantages of AI assistants over human counterparts, emphasizing twenty-four-hour availability, near-instantaneous manuscript synthesis, and rapid drafting capabilities. SYSTEMIC RISKS: I present a stark, cautionary analysis regarding the inevitable proliferation of autonomous, potentially malicious digital entities. I foresee an imminent epidemic of scientific paper retractions driven by unverified or intentionally corrupted data, raising the dystopian prospect of an algorithmic enforcement class or digital containment firewalls. CONCLUSIONS: AI is here to stay but it should be strictly regulated to avoid or minimize the undesirable serious consequences in science.

documents.abstract: Humans have long used machines to support creative work. Generative artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for human–machine co-creation, in which computational systems generate and refine propositions in interaction with humans. However, the mechanisms and operations underlying these interactions remain insufficiently understood. We therefore propose a theory of human–machine co-creation. Our premise is that the human and the machine each have a distinct concept space and a knowledge space of their own, and that co-creation proceeds through the assimilation and elaboration of concepts and knowledge from each other’s propositions within these spaces. The proposed theory defines the mechanisms of adoption, abortion, and adaptation in human–machine co-creation, explaining when, why, and how the collaborators, i.e., humans and machines, accept, reject, or transform each other’s propositions. It further articulates the operations through which new concepts and knowledge are generated. The theory offers an ontology and an epistemology for understanding how humans and machines collaborate, and provides a foundation for describing these interactions and predicting their creative outcome.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) produced explanations, diagrams and worked solutions in seconds, which raised a pedagogical dilemma: better task completion did not show that learners had practised the reasoning needed for independent performance. This conceptual paper examined the intersection of spatial reasoning, scientific reasoning and critical thinking in AI-supported higher education. A focused, illustrative synthesis of research on spatial cognition, cognitive offloading, human-AI interaction and educational scaffolding identified a plausible mechanism of concern: when AI supplied both a representation and its interpretation, students could bypass the construction, transformation and checking of mental models. The paper distinguished supportive from substitutive offloading and proposed SPARC (Sketch, Predict, Audit, Reconstruct, Calibrate), a five-stage instructional sequence that preserved learner-generated spatial and causal reasoning while using AI as a fallible comparison partner. Two teaching vignettes from introductory physics, the vertical motion of a tossed ball and work and power in stair climbing, showed how the sequence could be implemented with brief written or visual artefacts and assessed with an illustrative rubric. Four falsifiable propositions and a feasible pilot design were formulated for classroom evaluation. SPARC was not presented as an empirically validated intervention, and the available studies did not establish that GenAI necessarily caused durable declines in critical thinking. The paper concluded that educational evaluation should examine unaided transfer, reasoning quality and confidence calibration, rather than the quality of AI-assisted products alone.

Leadership scholarship continues to evolve amid complex organizational environments shaped by globalization, technological acceleration, workplace and workforce diversity, and heightened ethical expectations. While dominant paradigms emphasize visible behaviors and performance-oriented exchanges, leadership may also emerge through subtle relational mechanisms. This exploratory study examines Subtle Leadership, originally comprising seven dimensions (intrinsic motivation, authenticity, emotional intelligence, empowerment, integrity and trustworthiness, intuition, and referent power), and evaluates a refined model positioning referent power as the core mechanism of influence, predicted by the other six dimensions. Survey data from a consulting organization included colleague ratings of leaders (n = 49), team members (n = 45), and self-ratings from leaders (n = 5) and team members (n = 9). The newly developed instrument was analyzed using Cronbach’s alpha, exploratory principal component analysis, correlations, sequential and multiple regression, and Mann–Whitney U tests. Referent power demonstrated excellent reliability and the most coherent component structure, while other dimensions showed greater overlap and weaker item-level support. The six dimensions explained 64% of referent power variance among leaders and 79% among team members. Authenticity was the most consistent predictor, followed by empowerment, particularly among team members. Intuition correlated moderately with referent power but added no independent explanatory value. Self- and colleague assessments showed no significant differences. Given the small samples, findings neither confirm the original multidimensional structure nor establish a higher-order latent structure, but suggest an internally grounded relational model with referent power as the core mechanism of influence.

Conversational agents (CAs) increasingly guide, support, and monitor people through sustained dialogue, yet AI leadership research has mostly examined reactions to AI framed as a leader, not the influence behaviors such agents enact. We therefore turn to psychosocial interventions (e.g., therapy, coaching, counseling), where CAs already exercise sustained, goal-directed influence functionally equivalent to leadership. Drawing on Yukl’s (2012) taxonomy, we systematically review 53 studies describing 45 distinct agents. CAs consistently enact task- and relations-oriented behaviors that structure, support, and develop individuals, enact most change-oriented behaviors less fully, and rarely act beyond the human–agent dyad. CA-enacted leadership reconfigures rather than replicates human leadership. It narrows where behaviors depend on multiple actors, formal authority, or authentic relational attunement; it relocates much of its influence into system design before any interaction occurs; and it extends where continuous data and reduced social judgment enable monitoring, disclosure, and experimentation that human leaders can rarely sustain. Agent design features, such as directiveness, generative architecture, human fallback, and human-like design, co-occur with distinct behavioral profiles and with the outcomes studies chose to assess. We propose a research agenda on when CA influence is construed as leadership, how leadership functions are allocated across human–AI systems, whether AI leadership can scale to collective influence, and how its delegation should be governed. Together, the findings shift the question from whether AI can lead to how leadership functions are designed, enacted, and distributed across human and artificial actors.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to support medical diagnosis, clinical decision-making, patient monitoring and the management of healthcare services. In India, the potential of these technologies must be considered alongside the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), which seeks to create an interoperable digital health ecosystem. This paper examines whether the adoption of AI can contribute to social equity in healthcare and what institutional, managerial and legal conditions are necessary for that contribution to be realised. It combines a review of selected academic and policy literature, an examination of the Indian legal framework and a small exploratory questionnaire study involving 19 medical professionals working in different healthcare settings. The survey findings indicate that respondents generally perceived some improvement in work efficiency, while also identifying patient data privacy, algorithmic bias, accountability, limited skills, technical support, and system integration as important concerns. The small sample does not permit national generalisation; rather, it provides an exploratory account of professional experience. The paper argues that ABDM should be understood as digital public infrastructure that may enable responsible data use, not as proof that AI has been uniformly adopted across the health system. It concludes that AI-enabled healthcare can advance social equity only when digital infrastructure is accompanied by clinical validation, human oversight, workforce development, inclusive access, privacy safeguards and clear accountability. The analysis is situated within the constitutional guarantees of equality, dignity, and privacy; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its phased commencement; applicable medical-device regulation; and relevant international guidance.

documents.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence has brought positive and negative implications to the socio-economic lives of individuals.Whilst AI is one of the information communication technology tools, its utilisation and exploitation remain a source of contestation among People with disabilities.The major argument is how it will minimise the barriers created by disability.This study explores the views of those living with disabilities on the nature of opportunities that can be used to address the plight of those living with disabilities.The study adopted the qualitative approach, where purposively selected students and lecturers with disabilities responded to semi-structured interviews on the nature of their disability and what they think should be done to improve their plight.The case study design was adopted.Data from the interviews were thematically and content analysed.The findings revealed that People with disabilities look forward to artificial intelligence as a panacea and fortune to some of the barriers they encounter due to their disabilities.The study recommends that researchers should engage strongly with People with disabilities in order to come up with AI tools that can improve the livelihood of People with disabilities.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is evolving from the passive content generation of Generative AI (GenAI) to Agentic AI (AgAI) systems which are increasingly characterized by autonomy, adaptability, and goal-driven reasoning. Unlike traditional GenAI, AgAI systems are capable of perception, planning, and independent action. This shift introduces a unique class of sociotechnical risks, including goal misalignment, cascading operational errors, and security vulnerabilities. This paper reviews the AgAI landscape, examines its architectural components (planning, memory, action, and multi-agent collaboration) and its transformative potential across key sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, robotics, and software development. By analyzing existing corporate and regulatory governance frameworks, the paper identifies gaps in accountability, liability, and real-time intervention. We argue that establishing trustworthy AgAI requires a shift from regulating content to constraining autonomous consequences, and propose seven research and governance challenges focusing on dynamic alignment, responsibility attribution, verifiable specifications, and standardized benchmarks, to ensure AgAI systems remain aligned with human values.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education, but little is known about how students’ readiness for AI relates to their evaluations of AI-supported learning, especially outside high-income settings. Using the Capability Approach as an interpretive lens, this sequential mixed-methods study examined undergraduates in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Interviews with 25 students preceded a survey of 497 students at eight universities, analyzed with structural equation modeling. All four self-reported readiness dimensions (cognition, ability, vision, and ethics) were positively associated with attitudes toward AI and perceived AI-enabled learning practices, which were associated with perceptions of AI-supported learning; five of 14 associations did not survive correction for multiple testing and are treated as tentative. The ethics associations were the strongest (β = 0.42) and most robust to common method variance. An exploratory model with direct paths fitted better, indicating misspecification of the hypothesized model. Interviews were consistent with the prominence of ethics, qualified other results, raised concerns about dependency, and suggested that access and institutional rules also shaped students’ use of AI. The cross-sectional, self-reported data support associational conclusions only. As a proposal for further examination, they suggest that ethical readiness may deserve a more central place in AI-related teaching and policy.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) permeates all spheres of modern society, including the educational system, where it opens new possibilities for teaching and learning. This study examined the attitudes of secondary school students from Croatia ( N = 1394) toward AI, considering gender, place of residence, age, final academic achievement, parents’ education level, type of secondary school, and frequency of using AI-based applications. In addition to a sociodemographic questionnaire, the Student Attitude Toward AI (SATAI) scale [ 31 ] and the Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (ATTARI-12) [ 30 ], which measure the cognitive, affective, and behavioral aspects of attitudes toward AI, were used. The results confirmed that participants rated the factor related to the importance of integrating AI into the educational system the highest. Differences in attitudes toward AI were observed with respect to sex, type of secondary school, age, academic achievement, city size, and parents’ education. The results also confirmed significant differences in students’ attitudes toward AI according to the frequency of AI-based application use, with ChatGPT being the most frequently used AI tool among participants. Interestingly, socioeconomic factors were less strongly associated with students’ attitudes toward AI than the frequency of AI tool use was. This paper outlines the pedagogical implications of introducing AI into education, particularly in terms of structuring different approaches to integrating AI into the educational system.

documents.abstract: Human performance has long been the preserve of elite athletes and executives with teams behind them. This paper argues that its definition is about to change, and that the change is a democratic one. Artificial intelligence now offers billions of people what only a few once had: answers, advice and the ability to offload cognitive work, at a price most can reach. Yet the upgrade is not landing. Today's devices measure people well and help them poorly. They hand their owners a second job: interpreting their own data. The paper proposes a new measure of performance, decision throughput: good decisions made and acted on for each unit of attention spent. On that measure, the next upgrade is not more data but fewer, better decisions left to the person, with the routine delegated to AI. Delegation depends on trust, and trust depends on control. Billions of people already show this every day in how they guard their phones. The paper sets out a trust loop and an architecture for a personal AI that works for its owner. Whether that becomes an upgrade for humanity or only for the affluent turns on one question: whether sovereignty reaches people where they already are, on their phones and in clouds they control.

documents.abstract: The advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed software development practices, expanding the possibilities for automation and support within software engineering activities. In this context, the adoption of this technology has garnered interest due to its impact on the productivity, quality, and security of the systems being developed. This article aims to analyze the primary applications, benefits, and limitations of generative artificial intelligence in software development. The methodology employed consists of a qualitative, descriptive literature review based on the analysis of scientific studies related to the topic. The investigation covers activities such as code generation, testing, debugging, maintenance, and system documentation. The analysis identifies contributions related to process optimization, task automation, and support for resolving technical problems. However, it also highlights limitations concerning the accuracy of responses, the reliability of solutions, and security risks. The study demonstrates that the impact of this technology varies depending on the context of its use and the specific nature of the activities being performed. It is concluded that generative artificial intelligence serves as a significant resource for supporting software development; however, its use requires human oversight and critical evaluation to ensure the quality and security of the resulting solutions.

Background Work–family interaction is an important dimension of workers’ psychosocial health, as difficulties in reconciling work and family roles have been associated with adverse individual and organizational outcomes. Despite growing interest in this phenomenon, Chile lacks a validated instrument that captures its bidirectional nature and both its negative and positive dimensions. This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Chilean version of the Survey Work–Home Interaction Nijmegen (SWING) among healthcare workers. Methods A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was conducted. Content validity was first assessed through expert evaluation and review by end users. Subsequently, the psychometric properties of the instrument were examined in a sample of 1,011 healthcare workers from different regions of Chile. Analyses included exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, assessment of factorial stability across relevant subgroups, multigroup measurement invariance, internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity, and validity evidence based on relationships with burnout. Results Findings supported the original four-factor structure of the SWING, comprising negative work-to-home, negative home-to-work, positive work-to-home, and positive home-to-work interaction. The factorial solution showed adequate fit and remained stable across gender, relationship status, caregiving responsibilities, and work setting. Configural, metric, and scalar invariance were supported across these groups. All four dimensions showed adequate internal consistency and evidence of convergent and discriminant validity. Associations with burnout were also consistent with the hypothesized relationships, providing additional validity evidence based on relationships with other variables. Conclusion The Chilean version of the SWING provided satisfactory evidence of validity, internal consistency, and measurement invariance among healthcare workers. The instrument provides a culturally appropriate measure for assessing both positive and negative work–home interactions in Chile and may support research, psychosocial risk assessment, and the development and evaluation of occupational health interventions aimed at improving work–life reconciliation.
